newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court convicts East Berlin spymaster Wolf.
newsitem.headline: German court convicts East Berlin spymaster Wolf.

text.p: Legendary former East German spymaster Markus Wolf was found guilty in a German court on Tuesday of three kidnappings during the Cold War and handed a two year suspended sentence.
The trial was the latest attempt to punish the suave man who ran East Germany's foreign intelligence network for over 30 years after a 1993 treason conviction was overturned in 1995.

Wolf was found guilty of organising the kidnapping of a Ministry for State Security (Stasi) official who had fled to the West and the abduction of a West Berlin secretary whom the authorities hoped to persuade to spy for the East.
The court said Wolf, 74, was also behind the arrest of an East German whom the Stasi tried to force to sign defamatory statements about former Chancellor Willy Brandt, then mayor of West Berlin.
"I suppose I should be able to live with this," Wolf told a news conference after the judgement was read out, noting that prosecutors had demanded a three-and-a-half year jail term.
Wolf has denied all the charges and said he was being punished by what he called a political trial as a substitute for bringing to book former communist East German leaders.
"This was a political trial," he said, "Every agent in both East and West could be prosecuted for kidnapping."
But chief judge Ina Obst-Oellers said the Duesseldorf court had found Wolf guilty of four counts of kidnapping, two of coercion and two of bodily harm.
"I want to firmly set it straight that he was not convicted because he was a Stasi symbol," Obst-Oellers told the court in the two-hour judgement. "He was accused of concrete crimes."

Wolf was convicted of treason at the same court in 1993. But Germany's highest court overturned the ruling in 1995, saying he could not be convicted for spying for East Berlin on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.
This time prosecutors charged Wolf with crimes under East German law and three weeks ago dropped charges of treason and extortion against him to speed up the trial.

The elusive figure, who ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters, was dubbed "the man without a face" by his Western counterparts, who for decades had little idea what he looked like.
Thriller writers often took him as a model when depicting a sinister communist spy chief.
One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside then West German chancellor Willy Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
The three cases from the height of the Cold War in this attempt to punish Wolf could certainly have figured in any respectable spy thriller.
In 1962 a Stasi officer was demoted over a love affair of which his superiors disapproved. The officer, Walter Thraene, fled to Austria.
But Stasi officers lured him and his girlfriend to a hideout, beat him unconscious and spirited them back to East Berlin. Thraene spent over 10 years in jail, his girlfriend three.

Wolf denies having known of that operation, but his signature does appear on the 1955 order to try to recruit Christa Trapp, a German translator at the U.S. High Commission in West Berlin. Trapp was abducted to East Berlin but refused to sign up as a spy and was sent home the next day.

And Wolf makes no secret of having ordered the detention in 1959 on fabricated charges of Georg Angerer, an East German typesetter who worked in Nazi-occupied Norway in World War Two as interpreter for the Gestapo secret police.

The aim was to make Angerer sign defamatory statements about Brandt, then mayor of West Berlin, who spent some time in Norway during the war. Wolf says he genuinely suspected that Brandt had been a Gestapo agent.
Angerer was released after six months -- according to the prosecution, a broken man.
